content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper builds on recent work to build large language models trained directly on acoustic speech data rather than text - generative spoken language models (GLSM).  The speech data is encoded in short units of around 10 to 20 msecs and the signal is reconstructed by sampling the inventory of units in a similar manner to the text case.  The novelty of the work described here is that the input unit size is increased to 200ms or more to make the units more comparable to words.  This is done by encoding the sequence of frames in each input unit as a speech sequence unit.  However, the encoding of each SSE is now effectively continuous with several implications, in particular, reconstruction is no longer possible by sampling from a fixed inventory.   It also turns out that a much wider segment of speech influences each 200ms unit, and since the implied units are no longer independent, generation is no longer possible by concatenating units.    To solve these problems, the authors introduce a so-called 'lexical embedding' layer between the acoustic input units and the LM transformer.  This layer includes a PCA based vector quantiser which acts as a bottleneck filtering out most of the contaminating acoustic context.   The results show similar performance to existing GSLMs with the claimed advantage that the longer units improve efficiency and enable the transformer to learn wider contexts.  Intriguingly, when the input audio is segmented at word boundaries (using an oracle), the performance is much improved but these improvements are lost when using an automatic word boundary detector.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The paper gives some interesting insights into the tradeoffs between different acoustic unit sizes and methods of sampling when there is no discrete unit inventory.  However, the results obtained do not improve on the SoTA and the lexical embedding layer feels like a hack.  Otherwise there is little that is really original in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to read but quite hard to follow in detail.  There are no formal definitions of any of the operations and I would struggle to reproduce this system from the information given.  Understanding is not helped by the broken figure references.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall,  this paper feels preliminary and needs further work.  The results are not compelling and bottleneck vector quantiser needs clearer motivation.

content.title: Answer to Reviewer cDup
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback.

Here is the list of your main concerns and our responses:

$\bullet$ Figure indexing is wrong and some typographic errors

We corrected the figure indexing as well as other typographic errors. 

$\bullet$ Add formal definitions of the computation of q as well as clearer motivations

We added the Appendix A.1 to clarify the computation of q and motivate its presence.

$\bullet$There is little that is really original in the paper

We all know how to train a language model on discrete tokens. Yet, using continuous inputs with a virtually infinite latent vocabulary requires major changes at almost every level of the pipeline: the loss, the generation method and the decoding into speech. We think that our sampling strategy that uses a k-NN search is truely novel. All language models so far have do sampling on word types whereas we propose to sample on pseudo-word tokens (our 200ms units) where all instances of pseudo-words are stored as a distinct memory trace. We did not expect that method to work that well. The quality of the generation demonstrate the semantic and syntactic quality of the learned lexical tokens.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new generative spoken language modeling (GSLM) technique, tGSLM, which uses larger, word-size audio tokens taking inspiration from text based language models (LM). To build a text-like LM, a new lexical unit discovery method is used, which combines PCA and k-means to generate quantized embeddings for speech units. A causal LM is trained using NCE loss and at test time, a kNN search on a cached database produces the next token. Results are shown on generation quality and zero-shots tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. A new, interesting technique for generating lexical tokens from audio units
2. Evaluation is done on a variety of tasks.
3. Different segmentation techniques are compared with the simple 200ms approach. These are good baselines which outline the effectiveness of a simpler approach.
4. The paper studies the interpretability of the acoustic and lexical tokens which is a major contribution of this paper. Some of the claims in section 3.1.2 are substantiated in this study.
5. Audio examples are made available on an anonymous website.
6. The authors are committed to releasing their code.

Weaknesses:

1. The proposed models will have low latency during generation, which is a good thing but the authors do not provide any numbers for the same. I agree that the sequence length has been dramatically reduced. But the question is whether using wav2vec2.0 itself makes sequence length reduction at a later stage redundant? Maybe not, but having a quantification of  FLOPs/latency of generation would put the results into a larger perspective.
2. Maybe I am missing something but using wav2vec2.0 seems rather counterintuitive for a generation task. Wav2vec2.0 is a bidirectional model and the authors “encode a full speech sentence” using it. How is it used at test time when the entire speech is not available. This is not very clear from the text. Also, how does using wav2vec2.0 make the model memory efficient? Again, a quantification of memory requirements will benefit the paper.
3. The authors use PCA to overcome the problem of information leakage from wav2vec2.0. But, something as simple as using log-mel features or MFCC features from 200ms audio would overcome this problem as these classical techniques are more local feature extractors than wav2vec2.0 which uses self-attention over the entire speech. The authors do not report the effect of this simple approach. Does it degrade performance? It would be useful to have those numbers as a baseline.
4. Regarding lexical token generation, it is not clear how the number of basis vectors for PCA are chosen. Also, for k-means, the authors say, “... we set to K the numbers of clusters in the first PCA dimension … ”, what does this mean? Is K the number of clusters in k-means? If so, how is it chosen? 
5. It is not clear lexical tokens corresponding to which k-means clustering are stored in the cache, as from my understanding, k-means is run for each dimension of the PCA-reduced features.
6. Effect of the proposed model on downstream tasks like speech-to-speech translation is missing.
7. The paper could benefit immensely from proofreading. In many places, the authors refer to the wrong figure. For example, in the beginning of section 3.1.1, the authors refer to figure 3 instead of figure 1.  In section 3.2.1, they refer to figure 3.2 instead of figure 2. In section 5.1, they refer to figure 5 instead of figure 3. This makes for a confusing reading experience.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. The paper has some clarity issues in regards to the lexical embedding generation. Specifically, why PCA is used. (See points 3 and 4 in weaknesses)
2. The quality of the paper can be improved by fixing some typos.
3. The techniques proposed are novel to the best of my knowledge.
4. The authors are committed to releasing their code which hopefully will make the results reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a novel generative spoken language modeling (GSLM) technique. Although the authors conduct experiments on different datasets with different tasks, the paper lacks in some aspects of explaining their techniques properly. Specifically, in the lexical embedding generation technique, although the approach used seems ingenious, not enough explanation is given for the use of PCA on wav2vec2.0 embeddings. Specifically, certain simpler baselines are not included in the paper like using log-mels and MFCC for dealing with acoustic information leakage. Moreover, the main premise of the paper, which is a memory efficient model with competitive performance, remains incomplete due to the absence of numbers indicating reduction in model parameters / reduced latency / reduced FLOPs. These numbers will quantify how much memory efficiency is actually improved compared to previous models as performance-wise, 200ms-tGSLM does not do too much better (in some cases even worse) than GSLM. Also, does the use of wav2vec2.0 which itself is memory intensive defeats the purpose of reducing sequence length at a later stage? What are the effects on downstream tasks like speech-to-speech translation? These are some of the questions that remain unanswered.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4033 by Reviewer MqMZ

content.title: Answer to reviewer MqMZ
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback.

Here is the list of your main concerns and our responses:

$\bullet$ Figure indexing is wrong and some typographic errors.

We corrected the figure indexing as well as other typographic errors. 

$\bullet$ Can we get a FLOPs evaluation of the model to support the claim of memory efficiency?

We prove our claim that 200ms-tGSLM is 5 times more memory efficient with an experiment in Section 5.5. Specifically, we show that our model can be trained on a batch size that is 5 times bigger than GSLM’s maximal batch size. We support our experiment with a mathematical analysis of transformer memory usage in Appendix A.5.

$\bullet$ Does using Wa2vec2.0 make the sequence length reduction at a later stage redundant?

Wav2vec2.0 is used as a preprocessing step as part of the construction of the acoustic tokens. Therefore it does not impact the memory consumption at training time which is our main concern. Indeed if we want to reduce memory usage during training, it is to be able to train the LM on longer sentences to learn longer semantic dependencies. We made that point clearer in Section 3.1.1 and in Section 5.5. 

$\bullet$ If Wav2vec2.0 encodes a whole sentence, how can a sentence be generated when the entire speech is not available?

At inference time, we pre-extract acoustic and lexical tokens from a speech corpus and store them in a database. Also the lexical tokens are indexed in a k-NN graph. When we sample a continuation for a prompt, we sample a lexical token from the k-NN graph, and retrieve its corresponding acoustic tokens from the pre-extracted database. We made that point clearer in the Figure 3.

$\bullet$ If the attention mechanism in Wav2vec2.0 interfere with the language modelling loss, why not using more local features like Mel-filterbanks and/or MFCC to build the acoustic tokens?

We make that point clearer in the Appendix A.1: “We argue, that even though MFCC and  Mel-filterbanks are still good for supervised tasks as ASR, they are substantially outperformed by recent self-supervised speech models (Wav2vec2.0, CPC, HuBERT,...) at the tasks of zero-shot word discrimination and key-word spotting. Therefore, we think Mel-filterbanks and MFCCs are ill-suited to be the input of acoustic tokens.”

replying_to: Replying to Answer to reviewer MqMZ

content.title: Further comments
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their reply.

Regarding MFCC v/s wav2vec2.0, I am not convinced that MFCC/LFB features don't even merit a baseline just because they have been outperformed by recent deep models on certain tasks. This is because the authors are using PCA+k-means to mitigate some of the harmful artifacts of wav2vec2.0 which can be easily bypassed using MFCC/LFB. Whether it performs well or not still remains to be seen. There is no evidence currently to show that a dimension reduction (which would definitely result in information loss) is better than MFCC/LFB.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
In order to address the boundary problem and the clustering problem in speech models, this paper proposes to build a continuous tokenizer to avoid boundary detection or clustering step. 

Built upon the Generative Spoken Language Model (GSLM, https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01192), this paper feeds word-size continuous-valued tokens instead of discrete units into the language model (LM) by: 1) increasing the units to 200ms (from 20ms or 40ms) so that it's closer to word's length in speech; 2) encoding the outputs of the speech-to-unit (quantizer) encoder, wave2vec 2.0 in this paper, with speech sequence embedding model to obtain embeddings from the discrete unit, and pass the acoustic embeddings again to a lexical embedding layer to obtain lexical embeddings. 

To train the LM with continuous input (embeddings), the paper applies NCE loss. After generating a potential next lexical token embedding, the paper adopts the top-k sampling methods and samples one element from its K-NN. The sampling space is built with the lexical token embeddings from unseen speech sequences during training. 

This paper compares the proposed 200ms-tGSLM with GSLM and performs some ablation studies on both generation tasks and two zero-shot tasks. Results show that the proposed model reaches comparable results on zero-shot tasks with GSLM and achieves slightly better(lower) PPX on generation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The idea of this paper is straightforward and easy to understand. The motivation is compelling. 
2. The model is well-designed and the paper proposes various tricks to address certain issues.
3. The evaluation methods are reasonable. 
4. The demo page is clear and the quality of the generated speech is good. 

Weaknesses:

1. The writing of this paper can be improved. For example, the paper can use a lot less verbal description of the input and output of the model and defines variables so that it's easier for the reader to follow; the figures of the model (Figure 1) should be more clear; and there're some errors in the Figure references, in the beginning of section 3.1.1, I suppose the author means Figure 1 instead of Figure 3?

2. Indeed the paper proposes reasonable tricks to address certain issues but does not provide evidence for the choices of tricks. For example, why 200ms? Have you compared 50ms, 100ms and 300ms? It's understandable that 200ms is closer to a word's length than 40ms but why not 300ms? And for the LM prediction part, the paper proposes to predict the next three words and uses three heads instead of predicting merely the next word, due to a claimed reason that it's easy to predict the next word by just attending to very local acoustic information at the end of the last word. It's true that for short frames such as Mel, it's common to predict the next three to overcome the short-term invariance. For a 200ms sequence, does it necessary to predict three? It will be great to see some ablation studies on these choices as well.  

3. The improvements of the proposed methods compared to GSLM are marginal. In fact, in Table 1 and Table 2, the proposed 200ms-tGSLM performs slightly worse than the discrete version of GSLM, and even for the ppx of the generation task, 200ms-tGSLM is worse than GSLM on LibreSpeech and better than GSLM on LJ. It's hard to see the benefits of having continuous embeddings as inputs rather than discrete units. Although it's true that continuous embeddings may magically learn some mapping from audio units with bad boundaries to word tokens but it's not shown in this paper. Perhaps the author should design some tasks or use some examples to demonstrate this. 

4. It seems that the quality of the generated speech by 200ms-tGSLM is slightly better than GSLM, it's better to have some human eval to have a concrete conclusion.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity is acceptable. The quality can be improved. For technical novelty, most of the new components of the GSLM are adopted from existing works. The novelty mainly lies in introducing the idea of using continuous embeddings instead of discrete tokens.

I believe it's possible to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I like the idea of encoding the discrete units to continuous embeddings to overcome the issues of boundaries and clustering problems. And the proposed model is very reasonable. However, the paper needs more ablation studies to prove its choices of tricks and needs more analysis of the benefits of having word-size continuous-valued tokens. I think that improving the writing, adding some ablation study, and including human eval will improve the quality of the paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback.

Here is the list of your main concerns and our responses:

$\bullet$ Figure indexing is wrong, some typographic errors and introduce some variables make it easier to read.

We corrected the figure indexing as well as other typographic errors. We introduced notations and variables throughout the paper to facilitate reading. 

$\bullet$ Why 200ms per units? 

We added a gridsearch on the size of the units in Appendix Table 5 as well as a paragraph in Section 5.2. The gridsearch shows that 200ms is a good compromise between best performances on zero-shot tasks and largest unit duration.

$\bullet$ Why predict the next 3 units instead of only one?

We added a gridsearch on the number of prediction heads in Appendix Table 6. The gridsearch shows that 3 heads maximizes the performances on zero-shot tasks.

$\bullet$ What is the benefit of our method if performances with GSLM are alike?

We prove our claim that 200ms-tGSLM is 5 times more memory efficient with an experiment in Section 5.5. Specifically, we show that our model can be trained on a batch size that is 5 times bigger than GSLM’s maximal batch size. We support our experiment with a theoretical analysis of transformer memory usage in Appendix A.5.

$\bullet$ Could we have a human evaluation of generated sentences?

We did not have enough time to produce human evaluations before the deadline.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops a generative spoken language model based on learning large word-sized continuous units instead of small discrete units as in prior works. The prosed approach replaces all three units of language models by replacing the lookup table with a semi-learnable lexical embedding function, replacing the CE loss with a cross-entropy loss since the number of tokens is now virtually infinite, and replacing multinomial sampling by K-NN sampling. The authors conducted relatively comprehensive experiments on speech generation tasks and zero-shot challenge tasks and found tGSLM performs comparably with GSLM using discrete units, while achieving 5x memory reduction and learning phonetically and semantically interpretable units.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1.	The main innovation of this paper includes developing a spoken language modeling approach using large word-sized continuous units instead of small discrete units, as in prior works. The proposed approaches use 200ms long units, which could achieve 5x memory reduction compared to discrete units. Also, the proposed approach learns a mapping from acoustic space with phonetic properties to lexical space with syntactic and semantic properties, which enables learning both phonetically and semantically interpretable representations. These innovations and findings are meaningful and could inspire the community to explore more in this direction.

2.	The experiments are relatively comprehensive. The authors evaluate the proposed tokenGSLM  on speech generation and zero-shot challenges to interpret what spoken LM learns.

3.	The analysis on impact of speech segmentation is interesting. It shows that although true word boundaries could significantly improve tGSLM on speech generation and zero shot challenges (Table 1), using the two unsupervised speech segmentation models didn’t help tGSLM. This analysis points out the importance of exploring unsupervised speech segmentation models that can combine segmented units into intelligible speech.

4.	The ablation on q is useful and it aligns with the intuition that a low-variance signal in acoustic tokens interferes with syntactic and semantic modeling.  Also, the same trend is observed on both 200ms-tGSLM and gold-tGSLM.

Weaknesses:

1.	Some important insights and details are missing: (1) Please provide insights on why the naïve method of placing a boundary 200ms could work comparably with more complex speech segmentation systems. (2) Please provide insights on the zero-shot challenge results in Table 1, explain why GSLM performs better on two zero-shot tasks  sWUGGY and sBLIMP while 200ms-tGSLM  shows advantage on the other two zero-shot tasks ABXsem and ABXPOS.  Also on speech generation tasks, GSLM outperforms tGSLM on PPX@LS-VERT  while tGSLM outperforms GSLM on PPX@LJ-VERT , which is not explained clearly.

2.	Many references of figures and tables in the paper are wrong. It’s probably because for some figures/tables, the authors didn’t put the labels under the corresponding captions in latex.

3.	The English presentations have many problems and really need to be improved.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty: I find the main ideas novel and interesting. I also think this is the first work that develops an effective generative language model based on word sized continuous units.

Reproducibility: The paper did not provide a codebase, but the authors provide sufficient implementation details in Appendix A.1.

Clarity: 
Some details are missing in the presentation, for example,
(1)	Section 3.2.1, please provide more details on “speech sequences unseen during training”. 

References of some figures and tables are wrong, for example,
(1)	Section 3.1,  “The general structure of tGSLM is presented in Figure 3. “ It should be Figure 1, not Figure 3. 
(2)	“Figure 5 provides a comparison of the original discrete unit-based GSLM with two version of our continuous unit model: “ It should be Figure 3 instead.

The English presentations have many grammar issues. For example,
(1)	Introduction, there should NOT be a comma between “more difficult to solve than the first one ” and (Dunbar et al., 2022) 
(2)	“side steps” changes to “sidesteps”
(3)	There shouldn’t be a comma in “Having a continuous tokenizer, instead of a discrete one”
(4)	Section 2, “in a next step” probably changes to “in the next step”
(5)	Section 2, “The Zerospeech Challenge 2019” probably changes to “For the Zerospeech…”
(6)	Section 2, “probe spoken LMs learn” probably changes to “probe learned spoken LMs”
(7)	Section 3.1.2, “large as the size of the vocabulary” probably changes to “with the same size of the vocabulary”
(8)	Section 3.1.2, “potentially information” probably changes to “potential information”
(9)	This is not a grammatical sentence “A prob- lem already encountered in Algayres et al. (2022a); van den Oord et al. (2018) that is dealt with by sampling the negative tokens from the same speaker as the positive tokens. “
(10)	This sentence needs to be reordered “On the resulting batch of text is computed a pair of scores, called PPX/VERT. “
content.summary_of_the_review: I found the main ideas of the paper interesting and novel.  The proposed tokenGSLM explores large word-sized continuous units to replace previous small discrete units. To achieve this, the authors explore effective methods to replace all three elements of LMs. The experiments are relatively comprehensive to prove the proposed approach is comparable with GSLM with discrete units on speech generation and zero-shot challenges. Ablation further shows the usefulness of the proposed q, impact of speech segmentation and performance on interpretability.  On the other hand, some important insights and details are missing. The paper also has many clarity and presentation problems.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: General comment
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their feedback and suggestions. This helped improve our submission and better support our claims. We summarize here the main changes brought to the manuscript. 

$\bullet$ Addressing a concern of all reviewers, we corrected the figure indexing as well as other typographic errors. 

$\bullet$ We added a clearer explanation of the q function and a detailed formulation to ensure correct replication (Appendix A.1). 

$\bullet$ We ablated our choice of 200ms for unit durations as well as the 3 prediction heads (Appendix Table 5 and 6). 

$\bullet$ We improved the results' interpretation regarding the scores at the zero-shot and generation tasks. We also comment on why unsupervised speech segmentation does not lead to better generation than the 200ms units (Section 5.1 and 5.2).   

$\bullet$ Finally, our claim to reduce memory consumption is now supported with an experiment and a theoretical analysis of transformer memory usage (Section 5.4). 

We did our best to address the main concerns raised by reviewers and we hope that these improvements will be taken into consideration. To better highlight the changes brought to our manuscript, they appear in blue in the revised manuscript. Under acceptance, we will revert this change in color. We also answer each reviewer separately below.
